Iraq's government confirmed the attack originated from its soil; Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed a commander and ordered an investigation into the operations command in Maysan province, bordering Iran, and Iraq shut three border crossings to Iran, while pledging not to retaliate. Saudi Arabia said it too would not retaliate but wants Iraq to take necessary measures; Iraq is reportedly under US pressure to rein in Iran-backed militias. Trump said he believes Iran was probably behind the pipeline attack, while separately predicting the Iran war will end soon after the mid-term elections and that oil prices will then fall sharply. This compounds the crisis triggered by the Houthi rebels' rapid seizure of Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline, including the port of Mocha and the strategic Perim (Mayun) island commanding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the claiming of Zuqar island, and attacks on the Hanish islands -- more than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded and tens of thousands displaced in the fighting. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree declared Red Sea shipping safe for all vessels except Saudi ships. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has personally pressed Trump to launch direct military action against the Houthis as the advance threatens Yemen's fragile truce and Saudi Arabia itself. With both Bab el-Mandeb and now an alternative Saudi pipeline route imperiled alongside fears for the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices remain elevated but retreated Friday on hopes of renewed negotiations after notching sharp weekly gains, borrowing costs are rising, global markets are rattled including a six-week low on Australia's ASX, US gas prices remain at record highs, and Trump's Iran deal push is further complicated.
